title: Wire: from the Divi Blasii Font to the Fulton Ferry Slip
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mühlhausen, baptized at Divi Blasii
stops.date_confidence: 12 June 1806 attested in both the German and the English biographical record. The baptism at Divi Blasii is reported by the National Park Service biography.
stops.campa: A son is born in Mühlhausen, a walled Thuringian town lately absorbed into the Kingdom of Prussia, and is baptized in the Lutheran church of Divi Blasii as Johann August Röbling. The pointed Gothic openings of that church are claimed, long after his death, as the ancestors of the arches he cuts in his last towers over the East River. He never says so himself. He leaves Mühlhausen at fifteen for a mathematics tutor in Erfurt and comes back twice: once to write a thesis he never defends, once to arrange his departure from Europe.
suggested_refs: The Lutheran church of Divi Blasii, Mühlhausen, and the memorial plaque on the birth house
de.wikipedia.org, 'Johann August Röbling', on the plaque and the anglicization of the name

stops.name: Erfurt, three years with Unger
stops.date_confidence: June 1820 entry and 1823 departure per immigrantentrepreneurship.org, which quotes his own note that he 'passed my 1st Examination and returned to Mühlhausen in 1823'. An older account dating the start to 1821 is contradicted by that autobiographical line. Coordinates are the centroid of Erfurt: the institute building is not located here.
stops.campa: At fifteen he is sent down the road to Erfurt and enters the private mathematical institute of Ephraim Salomon Unger. The subjects are mathematics, surveying, and the field instruments that turn a hillside into numbers; architecture is not among them. He learns to arrive before the work with a chain and a level, and to write down what the ground actually is rather than what the drawing wants it to be. He stays three years and passes his first examination in 1823. He comes home to Mühlhausen at eighteen a qualified Feldmesser, licensed to measure land.
suggested_refs: Ephraim Salomon Unger's private mathematical institute at Erfurt, later the Königliche Gewerbeschule

stops.name: Berlin, the Royal Building Academy
stops.date_confidence: 1824 enrolment attested; month and day defaulted. A competing account has him finishing engineering studies at a 'Berlin-Charlottenburg Polytechnic' by 1826, which cannot be right: the Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg was founded in 1879. The pin marks Schinkel's Bauakademie building at the Werderscher Markt, finished in 1836, after his time.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Royal Building Academy in Berlin under Martin Friedrich Rabe, Johann Friedrich Dietlein and Johann Albert Eytelwein, the last of these the Prussian authority on hydraulics and the author of a Handbuch on the mechanics of solid bodies. Chains under load are in that book, forty years before there is an East River to hang one over. The Academy as yet has no building of its own; Schinkel's red brick block at the Werderscher Markt is twelve years from being finished. Roebling is eighteen and stays about two semesters.
suggested_refs: Johann Albert Eytelwein's Handbuch der Mechanik fester Körper und der Hydraulik, the hydraulics teaching of the Bauakademie

stops.name: Berlin, the lectures of Hegel
stops.date_confidence: attendance at Hegel's lectures during the Berlin studies is attested in the English Wikipedia biography and in immigrantentrepreneurship.org; no term or date is given, and October 1824 is set only to place the stop inside the Berlin year. The pin is the University of Berlin lecture-hall coordinate inherited unchanged from hegel.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the same city and the same year he crosses to the university on Unter den Linden to hear Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, six years into the chair of philosophy and near the height of a Berlin tenure that ends only with his death in the cholera autumn of 1831. For the next forty-five years Roebling writes philosophy alongside the working life, thousands of pages of it, most of it argument with Hegel about spirit and matter. None of it is published while he lives. What he made of the lectures while he was sitting in them, at eighteen, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: hegel.journey.json, the Berlin chair, 1818-1831
The unpublished Roebling philosophical manuscripts, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute MC 04 and Rutgers Roebling Family Collection

stops.name: Eslohe, the military roads of the Sauerland
stops.date_confidence: Prussian service in the Arnsberg district from about 1825 for roughly four years, attested by immigrantentrepreneurship.org; month and day defaulted. Coordinates corrected to the town of Eslohe itself, 51°15'N 8°10'E; an earlier figure placed the pin some seven kilometres north in open country.
stops.campa: He enters Prussian state service in the Arnsberg administrative district and is posted into the Sauerland hills, where for about four years he lays out and supervises military roads through country that resists them. The work is honest and the ceiling is low: a young engineer in Prussian service builds what the ministry orders, in the order the ministry decides. In his own hours he draws suspension bridges over the Ruhr and the Lenne, spans nobody commissions and nobody builds. The drawings go into a drawer and cross an ocean with him.
suggested_refs: The unbuilt Ruhr and Lenne suspension bridge sketches of the Westphalian years

stops.name: Mühlhausen, the thesis never defended
stops.date_confidence: the 1829 return and the abandoned second state examination are attested; month and day defaulted. The frequently repeated claim that police surveillance personally drove him out of Prussia is tradition and is not carried here as fact.
stops.campa: Back in his own town he prepares a thesis for the second state engineering examination, the gate into a permanent Prussian career, and does not sit it. The July Revolution of 1830 tightens censorship across the German states, and a certified surveyor with a drawer of unbuildable bridges concludes that Prussia has no use for him. He reads the emigration literature instead and corresponds with men planning German colonies in America. He falls in with Johann Adolphus Etzler, a utopian writer from his own town, at work on a book promising that machinery will shortly abolish labor altogether.
suggested_refs: Johann Adolphus Etzler, The Paradise within the Reach of all Men, without Labour, by Powers of Nature and Machinery (1833)

stops.name: Bremen, aboard the August Eduard
stops.date_confidence: 11 May 1831 departure, the ship's name, the 75-thaler cabin fare and the eleven-week crossing all from immigrantentrepreneurship.org; English Wikipedia gives 22 May for his leaving Prussia, which is a different act. Bremen was a sovereign Free Hanseatic City and never Prussian; an earlier draft of this dossier called it 'Bremen, Prussia'. City-centre pin.
stops.campa: He sails from Bremen, a sovereign Hanseatic city that is not Prussia and never has been, aboard the ship August Eduard, with his brother Carl and with Etzler and a party of emigrants who mean to found a colony together. Somewhere in the middle of the Atlantic Etzler's followers fall out with Etzler, and the colony is finished before the coast is sighted. The cabin fare is seventy-five thalers, about fifty-eight dollars. The crossing is expected to take six weeks and takes eleven.
suggested_refs: Roebling's own emigration diary of the 1831 crossing, Rutgers Roebling Family Collection

stops.name: Philadelphia, the landing on the Delaware
stops.date_confidence: 3 August 1831 per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; the Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid gives 6 August. The conflict is left standing. The pin is the Delaware River waterfront rather than Philadelphia City Hall, which sits about 1.5 km inland and had been used in the underlying dossier.
stops.campa: The August Eduard comes up the Delaware and puts its passengers ashore at Philadelphia after eleven weeks at sea. He is twenty-five, carries a surveyor's certificate no American authority recognizes, and does not yet speak the language of the country he has chosen. Two landing dates sit in the record, the third of August and the sixth, and the institution holding his family papers does not agree with the accounts that summarize them. He walks off the boat into a republic that will not employ him as an engineer for another nine years.
suggested_refs: Rutgers University Libraries, Roebling Family Collection finding aid, repositories/11/resources/908
sources: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid

stops.name: Butler County, fifteen hundred acres and a town called Germania
stops.date_confidence: the purchase of 1,582 acres from Mrs. Sarah Collins on 28 October 1831, and the Germania-to-Saxonburg renaming, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxonburg,_Pennsylvania, which also dates the founding to 1832. Coordinates corrected to the borough proper, 40°45'15"N 79°48'56"W; the dossier figure sat about 800 m northwest.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of October he buys some fifteen hundred and eighty-two acres of western Pennsylvania farmland from Mrs. Sarah Collins, north of Pittsburgh in Butler County, and lays the town out himself with the instruments he trained on at Erfurt. He calls it Germania. Within a year the settlers have renamed it Saxonburg. He surveys the streets and sells lots to arriving Germans, and for nine years nobody in America hires him to build anything. He farms the rest without much success. He keeps bees. In the evenings there is the flute.
suggested_refs: The original Roebling plat of Saxonburg, Butler County, Pennsylvania

stops.name: Saxonburg, marriage to Johanna Herting
stops.date_confidence: May 1836 per the Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid; day not established and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He marries Johanna Herting in the settlement he laid out, in a German-speaking town of his own making, four thousand miles from Mühlhausen. She keeps the household at Saxonburg and afterward at Trenton through nearly three decades in which he is mostly somewhere else, on canal banks and river gorges from Pittsburgh to Niagara. What survives from that household in any quantity is his own working correspondence and the philosophical manuscripts he wrote in the hours around it. The archives hold the month and the year of the wedding. The day is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection, family correspondence series
sources: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid

stops.name: Saxonburg, the birth of Washington Roebling
stops.date_confidence: 26 May 1837 per the Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid.
stops.campa: His first child is born at Saxonburg on the twenty-sixth of May and is named Washington Augustus, after the general whose republic the father has adopted. The boy will go to Rensselaer, join his father's practice at twenty-one, take a colonel's commission in the Union army, inherit an unbuilt East River bridge from a dead man in 1869, be crippled by caisson disease under the river, and finish the work from a window in Brooklyn Heights while his wife carries his orders to the site. It begins in a frame house in a German farm village in Butler County.
suggested_refs: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Roebling Collection MC 04, Washington A. Roebling papers
sources: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid

stops.name: Saxonburg, the death of Carl Röbling
stops.date_confidence: 1837 attested for Carl's death and for the return to engineering work; month and day are set only to order the stop between his son's birth in May and the naturalization in September.
stops.campa: His brother Carl dies, and the colony two men founded together becomes one man's burden. The farm has never paid, and the certificate from Erfurt has been folded in a drawer for six years while its owner sold lots to his countrymen on a hillside in Butler County. Roebling puts down the plough and takes the certificate to the canal and railroad offices of western Pennsylvania, looking for the profession he trained for at nineteen. He finds work on a canal survey in Ohio before the year is out. He is thirty-one years old.
suggested_refs: The Saxonburg burying ground and the early settler records of Butler County

stops.name: Butler County, the oath and the new name
stops.date_confidence: 30 September 1837 per de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_August_Röbling, which ties the naturalization to the anglicization of the name. The NPS page cited for this date in the underlying dossier carries no naturalization date at all. The court of record is not established; the pin is Saxonburg, not a courthouse.
stops.campa: He takes the oath of citizenship and in the same act changes his name. Johann August Röbling becomes John A. Roebling, the umlaut resolved into an English vowel, the Christian name translated. He is not hiding: he writes German to his family, reads German philosophy until the day he dies, and will be buried in New Jersey under the anglicized form. The date is the thirtieth of September 1837, and the German record keeps it more precisely than the American one does.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_August_Röbling, on the 1837 naturalization and name change

stops.name: Sandy and Beaver Canal, back on the level
stops.date_confidence: 1837 per the NPS biography; the month is set only to place the stop after the September naturalization. The coordinates are an approximate point along the canal route, not a worksite: the stretch he surveyed is not established.
stops.campa: Work comes first on the Sandy and Beaver Canal in eastern Ohio, a short and ill-starred line on which he is one engineer among several. He is measuring again, on foot, with a level and a rod, for a canal system already being outrun by the railroads that will kill it. It is the first American employment in the trade he was licensed for at eighteen, and it comes to him at thirty-one, six years after he landed. The exact stretch he worked is not established, and the canal was never finished as designed.
suggested_refs: The Sandy and Beaver Canal Company records, Ohio Historical Connection

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the hemp that keeps parting
stops.date_confidence: 1839 to 1840 for the railway surveys under Charles L. Schlatter, per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; month and day defaulted, and the pin is Pittsburgh rather than any single survey line. The widely repeated story that he personally saw two men killed by a snapping hemp rope is tradition; no contemporary accident report has been found.
stops.campa: He serves as principal assistant to Charles L. Schlatter on the Pennsylvania railway surveys, running lines across the Allegheny Mountains for a state that means to reach the Ohio from Philadelphia. On the Allegheny Portage Railroad the loaded canal boats are hauled up ten inclined planes on hemp hawsers, and the hemp fails. It rots, it frays, it parts under load and sends the boat back down the slope through whatever is behind it. Roebling has seen wire rope in Germany. He begins working out how to make it here, in a meadow, by hand.
suggested_refs: The Allegheny Portage Railroad inclined planes, Cambria County, Pennsylvania

stops.name: Philadelphia, the letter to Charles Ellet Jr.
stops.date_confidence: 28 January 1840 per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Roebling. The Fairmount competition and the patronage said to have decided it recur throughout the Roebling literature but were not confirmed against a primary source in this pass and are carried as tradition. The pin is the proposed Fairmount bridge site.
stops.campa: He writes to Charles Ellet Jr., the only man in America then building suspension bridges, offering himself as an assistant and setting out what he has been thinking about since Westphalia. Ellet answers, uses him, and beats him: to the Fairmount crossing at Philadelphia, to Wheeling, and eventually to the first contract at Niagara. The rivalry runs for the rest of Ellet's life and neither man ever wholly wins it. Of the Fairmount competition itself, and of the patronage said to have settled it, no document has been produced.
stops.quote: The study of suspension bridges formed for the last few years of my residence in Europe my favourite occupation ... Let but a single bridge of the kind be put up in Philadelphia, exhibiting all the beautiful forms of the system to full advantage, and it needs no prophecy to foretell the effect which the novel and useful features will produce upon the intelligent minds of the Americans.
stops.quote_source: Roebling to Charles Ellet Jr., 1840, as quoted in Steinman and Watson, Bridges and Their Builders (1941); seen only in Wikipedia's reproduction of that citation, the 1941 book and the original letter both unreached
suggested_refs: Charles Ellet Jr., the Fairmount and Wheeling suspension bridges
David B. Steinman and Sara Ruth Watson, Bridges and their Builders (1941)

stops.name: Saxonburg, the ropewalk in the meadow
stops.date_confidence: 1841 for the start of commercial wire rope production at Saxonburg; month and day defaulted. Coordinates are the borough pin: the ropewalk stood on his own farm, whose exact bounds are not mapped here.
stops.campa: In a field beside the farmhouse he builds a ropewalk, a long straight lane where wire is drawn out, laid parallel on trestles and twisted into cable. He designs the closing machine himself and puts his neighbors and his own household to work on it. What comes off the end is the first wire rope manufactured in the United States. It is sold by the foot, out of a Butler County meadow, by a man who has never run a factory, to canal companies who have hauled with nothing but hemp in their lives.
suggested_refs: The Roebling ropewalk site, Saxonburg, Pennsylvania

stops.name: Saxonburg, Patent No. 2,720
stops.date_confidence: 16 July 1842 confirmed directly at patents.google.com/patent/US2720A/en, issued to John A. Roebling of Saxonburg, Pennsylvania. The NPS biography independently dates the first test of the rope on Incline 3 of the Allegheny Portage Railroad to 1842. The sabotage story is reported and unconfirmed.
stops.campa: United States Patent 2,720, Method of and Machine for Manufacturing Wire Ropes, issues to John A. Roebling of Saxonburg, Pennsylvania. That same year his rope goes onto Incline 3 of the Allegheny Portage Railroad and holds where hemp did not. A story attaches to the trial and is repeated in the biographies: that a first demonstration was sabotaged, a rope cut by men whose trade the wire threatened, and that a second test had to be run before the canal commissioners would look at it. No contemporary account of the cutting has been found.
suggested_refs: US Patent 2,720, patents.google.com/patent/US2720A/en
Incline 3, Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site

stops.name: Pittsburgh, a canal crosses the Allegheny
stops.date_confidence: completed May 1845; the low bid among 44 is attested by immigrantentrepreneurship.org. Coordinates set at the foot of 11th Street, the Pennsylvania Canal crossing, to separate this structure from the Sixth Street bridge; the dossier had stacked both on one point. Note that the Wikipedia page titled 'Allegheny Aqueduct' is a different 1824 stone structure in Berks County.
stops.campa: The Pennsylvania Canal's wooden aqueduct over the Allegheny at the foot of Eleventh Street is rotten and must be replaced. Forty-four bids come in. Roebling's is the lowest and he is nobody. It is the first bridge he has ever been given to build. He puts up seven spans of about a hundred and sixty-two feet, each carrying a wooden trough full of canal water on two continuous wire cables of his own manufacture, and finishes in May 1845. The boats cross the Allegheny at the level they were travelling on before, in water, on wire.
suggested_refs: The Pennsylvania Canal aqueduct at Pittsburgh, 1845, demolished 1861

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the Smithfield Street crossing
stops.date_confidence: opened February 1846 per the NPS biography; day defaulted. Coordinates corrected to 40°26'5"N 80°0'8"W per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithfield_Street_Bridge, about 300 m from the dossier figure. This crossing is the Monongahela, not the Allegheny, despite a parenthetical in the underlying chronology calling it a road bridge over the Allegheny.
stops.campa: The Great Fire of 1845 takes Louis Wernwag's wooden bridge over the Monongahela, and the company hires the man who has just carried a canal over the Allegheny. He spans the river at Smithfield Street on wire cable and opens it in February 1846. Thirty-seven years later Gustav Lindenthal replaces the deck and the cables with a lenticular truss and leaves Roebling's stone piers standing in the water, where they are still standing. The Smithfield crossing is the Monongahela; the aqueduct was the Allegheny; the books confuse the two constantly.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithfield_Street_Bridge, on Wernwag's 1818 bridge and Lindenthal's 1883 replacement on Roebling's piers

stops.name: Minisink Ford, the Delaware Aqueduct
stops.date_confidence: begun 1847, opened 1849; month and day defaulted to 01 within the opening year. The companion Lackawaxen aqueduct, of which only abutments survive, stood about 41.477, -74.986, coordinates estimated from the confluence and not surveyed.
stops.campa: For the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company he hangs a suspension aqueduct over the Delaware itself, five hundred and thirty-five feet of trough on wire cable, begun in 1847 and open in 1849 at a cost of $41,750. Coal boats now cross above the rafts of the Delaware lumbermen instead of fighting them at a slackwater pool. A companion aqueduct over the Lackawaxen costs $18,650 and leaves only its abutments. The Delaware crossing survives whole, carries automobiles, and is the oldest wire suspension bridge in the United States.
suggested_refs: Roebling's Delaware Aqueduct, National Historic Landmark, nps.gov/upde

stops.name: Trenton, the works between the canal and the railroad
stops.date_confidence: operations running by October 1849 per the NPS biography; day defaulted. The land purchase is dated 1848 in some accounts and 1849 in others.
stops.campa: He buys ground at Trenton where the Delaware and Raritan Canal meets the Camden and Amboy Railroad and moves the wire business off the Saxonburg meadow into a factory, with Charles Swan as superintendent and the first operations running by October 1849. Saxonburg keeps the farmhouse and the name. The rope is no longer a sideline of a farm: it is a plant with a payroll, and it outlives him by a century, employs thousands, raises a company town downriver, and pays for the bridges on which he loses money.
suggested_refs: John A. Roebling's Sons Company, Trenton, New Jersey; the Kinkora Works at Roebling, New Jersey

stops.name: High Falls, the Rondout crossing
stops.date_confidence: completed in the latter half of 1850 per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; month set inside that half-year, day defaulted. The dossier tagged this as an unverified lead: it is attested twice, and the coordinates are corrected from a point nearly 10 km south to High Falls itself, 41°49'37"N 74°7'20"W.
stops.campa: The canal company wants the method repeated and he supplies it: a third crossing at High Falls in Ulster County, over the Rondout, finished in the second half of 1850. Nine years earlier no wire rope at all was made in this country. The design has become a kind rather than an invention, two cables and a wooden trough on stone anchorages, priced and delivered like a manufactured article rather than argued for from first principles each time. The hamlet stands around the water crossing and takes its name from the falls beside it.
suggested_refs: The Delaware and Hudson Canal at High Falls, New York, and the D&H Canal Museum

stops.name: Cuddebackville, the Neversink
stops.date_confidence: completed in the latter half of 1850 per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; the month orders it after High Falls and is not itself attested. Coordinates sit about 2 km southwest of Cuddebackville proper and are approximate.
stops.campa: The last of the four goes over the Neversink near Cuddebackville in the same season. From here the Delaware and Hudson Canal runs on Roebling cable at every difficult water in its length, and the company that hired an untried German for one experiment has bought the whole method. He is forty-four years old. He has still built nothing that a train can cross, and the railroads killing off his canal clients one by one are about to become the only clients he has.
suggested_refs: The Neversink Aqueduct site, Cuddebackville, Orange County, New York

stops.name: Niagara Falls, two decks over the gorge
stops.date_confidence: 1851 for the start of the work; month and day defaulted. The 1854 cholera outbreak in the workmen's camp is family and biographical tradition: the standard account of the bridge does not mention any outbreak, and it could not be confirmed in this pass.
stops.campa: Ellet takes the first Niagara contract, strings his line across the gorge by kite, and quarrels with the directors until they dismiss him. Roebling gets what is left: loaded trains over eight hundred feet of gorge, two hundred and forty feet above the water, at a time when every authority in Europe including Robert Stephenson holds that a suspension bridge cannot carry a railway at all. He builds two decks in one structure, rail above and road below, stiffened with trusses and with stays run down to the rock. In 1854 cholera goes through the workmen's camp, and the family accounts say he treated the sick himself.
suggested_refs: Robert Stephenson's Britannia tubular bridge, the rival answer to the same problem

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the report to the directors
stops.date_confidence: 1852 publication; month and day defaulted. Text read directly in the archive.org OCR of the report, identifier reportjohnaroeb01compgoog.
stops.campa: He writes the directors a report that is a manifesto as much as an accounting. The cables are described and the anchorages calculated at five times the greatest tension they will ever see, and the doubters are answered in the only public register he uses, which is that of a man who has already done the arithmetic. It is dated 1852, three years before there is a bridge for anyone to ride across. The document is printed and circulated, and engineers go on arguing with it for forty years.
stops.quote: Nothing is impracticable, which is within the scope of natural laws.
stops.quote_source: John A. Roebling, Report to the Directors of the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company (1852), archive.org identifier reportjohnaroeb01compgoog
suggested_refs: Report of John A. Roebling to the Directors of the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company, 1852, full text at archive.org

stops.name: Kentucky River, the bridge that is not built
stops.date_confidence: reported, not confirmed against a primary source in this pass. The crossing site is uncertain and the coordinates are approximate, taken near a later Kentucky River crossing. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He contracts to bridge the Kentucky River for a railroad that then collapses financially, and nothing is built. The drawings join the Ruhr and the Lenne in the drawer, twenty-eight years and an ocean later. The surviving Roebling bridges are the residue of a much larger number of Roebling proposals, and this one left no residue at all. Of the project the record is thin. The crossing site is not firmly established, and the design is not in any collection reached here.
suggested_refs: The unbuilt Kentucky River suspension bridge design, c. 1853
sources: John A. Roebling dossier, unconfirmed lead

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the locomotive on the upper deck
stops.date_confidence: 18 March 1855 for the official opening by a fully laden passenger train, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls_Suspension_Bridge, which also dates the 23-ton test locomotive 'London' to 8 March; immigrantentrepreneurship.org instead says the first train crossed on 16 March. The two accounts are left standing side by side. The lower deck had opened in 1854.
stops.campa: On the eighth of March a twenty-three-ton locomotive named London is run out onto the upper deck and held there, and the bridge takes it. Ten days later a fully laden passenger train crosses and the structure is open, though one account puts the first crossing on the sixteenth and the two dates have never been reconciled. The lower deck has been carrying carriages for a year. It is the first suspension bridge anywhere to carry regular railway traffic, and it does so for forty-two years, until the last of it is taken down in August 1897.
stops.quote: Whenever necessity calls for new works of art, new expedients will be discovered, adapted to the occasion. It will no longer suit the spirit of the present age to pronounce an undertaking impracticable.
stops.quote_source: John A. Roebling, Report to the Directors of the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company (1852), archive.org identifier reportjohnaroeb01compgoog
suggested_refs: The Whirlpool Rapids Bridge, which replaced it in 1897

stops.name: Niagara Falls, inspecting his own bridge
stops.date_confidence: the report is dated 1 August 1860; text read directly in the archive.org OCR, identifier reportonconditio00roeb.
stops.campa: Five years after the opening he inspects the bridge and reports that after a thorough examination of every part of the work he is unable to report any change. The five mile an hour limit on trains is not a confession of weakness, he writes, but the caution designed into the thing from the beginning; the cable iron he is unwilling to estimate at less than several hundred years of life. Then the report leaves its brief altogether and turns to iron itself, and to what a century that has learned to draw it into wire might do with it. The document is dated the first of August 1860.
stops.quote: Iron has emphatically become the material of the age. Upon its proper use the future comfort and physical advancement of the human race will principally depend.
stops.quote_source: John A. Roebling, Report on the Condition of the Niagara Railway Suspension Bridge, 1 August 1860, archive.org identifier reportonconditio00roeb
suggested_refs: Report on the Condition of the Niagara Railway Suspension Bridge, 1860, full text at archive.org

segments.name: The Ohio, the Allegheny, the Household

stops.name: Cincinnati and Covington, the contract on the border
stops.date_confidence: contract signed 18 April 1856 per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roebling_Suspension_Bridge, which also carries the Panic of 1857 and Civil War delays.
stops.campa: He signs on the eighteenth of April to carry a road across the Ohio between Cincinnati and Covington on a single span of one thousand and fifty-seven feet, longer than anything suspended anywhere on earth. The Panic of 1857 stops the money inside the first year. The war stops the rest, and the river he is bridging becomes the line between a slave state and a free one, with Kentucky's legislature disinclined to help Ohio reach it. The unfinished towers stand in the water for years, visible from both banks.
suggested_refs: The 1863 pontoon bridge thrown across the Ohio at Cincinnati during Kirby Smith's advance

stops.name: Pittsburgh, Sixth Street and a son in the office
stops.date_confidence: construction commenced spring 1858 and the bridge opened to traffic 2 May 1860, per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; the chronology's '1859 completion' is too early and 1857 starts appear in other accounts. Spans of 343 ft with 179 ft shore spans, dismantled 1892, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Clemente_Bridge, whose coordinates are used here.
stops.campa: Construction begins in the spring on his third and last Pittsburgh bridge, a stayed suspension crossing of the Allegheny at Sixth Street, two main spans of three hundred and forty-three feet with shore spans of a hundred and seventy-nine. In the same spring Washington Roebling, twenty-one and just out of Rensselaer, joins his father's office and is put to work on it; the partnership begun here runs eleven years and ends at a ferry slip in Brooklyn. The bridge opens to traffic on the second of May 1860 and is taken down in 1892.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Clemente_Bridge, the present structure on the Sixth Street site

stops.name: New York, Bridging the East River
stops.date_confidence: reported. The letter's title and argument recur throughout the Brooklyn Bridge literature, but no digitized copy was reached in this pass and the Wikipedia article on the bridge does not surface it. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He puts into print the argument he has been making privately for a decade: that the East River can be crossed, that the only two ways are a suspension bridge or a tunnel, that a bridge must hang high enough to leave the harbor traffic untouched, and that the work is better built on private capital than run by the city government. The letter is cited everywhere in the literature of the bridge. No copy of it was reached here. Seven years pass before anyone with money agrees with him.
suggested_refs: 'Bridging the East River', letter of 1860, cited throughout the Brooklyn Bridge literature and not located in this pass
sources: John A. Roebling dossier, publication reported and unverified

stops.name: Trenton, the death of Johanna
stops.date_confidence: 22 November 1864 at Trenton per the Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid, which states the place directly; the geography lens had treated Trenton as an assumption from the works' proximity, and that hedge can be dropped. The detail that he was away on business comes from immigrantentrepreneurship.org.
stops.campa: Johanna Herting Roebling dies at Trenton on the twenty-second of November after a long illness, twenty-eight years married. Her husband is away on business and does not reach her before the end. The finding aid that holds the family papers gives the place and the date; the circumstances come from elsewhere; the marriage itself is documented mostly in the intervals between his letters home. She had followed him from a Butler County farm village of his own surveying to a factory town on the Delaware, and the record of what she thought of either is not in the papers. He is fifty-eight.
suggested_refs: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid, on Johanna Herting Roebling

stops.name: Cincinnati and Covington, the longest span in the world
stops.date_confidence: opened to foot traffic 1 December 1866 and to general traffic 1 January 1867 per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roebling_Suspension_Bridge. The 1983 renaming rests on the dossier and on the bridge's public name; it was not independently confirmed in this pass.
stops.campa: After eleven years, a financial panic and a civil war, the Ohio bridge opens: to pedestrians on the first of December 1866, to everything else on the first of January. Its main span of one thousand and fifty-seven feet is the longest suspended span on earth. Cincinnati and Covington, which spent the war on opposite sides of the river and of the law, are joined by a structure begun before the fighting and finished after it. In 1983 it is renamed for the man who built it.
suggested_refs: The John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge, Cincinnati to Covington, renamed 1983

stops.name: Trenton, the second marriage and the manuscript pile
stops.date_confidence: February 1867, to Lucia W. Cooper of Trenton, per immigrantentrepreneurship.org; day defaulted, and the earlier hedge that the location was unconfirmed can be dropped. The length of the philosophical manuscripts is reported variously as roughly one thousand and roughly two thousand pages; the discrepancy is unresolved.
stops.campa: In February he marries Lucia W. Cooper of Trenton, two years and three months a widower, sixty years old. The record of this marriage is thinner than the record of the first. What is documented instead is the pile of manuscript in his study: cosmology, the fate of the soul, the unity of force and matter, Hegel and Swedenborg and the American spiritualist writers argued with at length in the same hand that elsewhere specifies cable diameters. How long the pile is has never been established. One count puts it near a thousand pages, another at twice that.
suggested_refs: The unpublished Roebling philosophical manuscripts, RPI MC 04 and the Rutgers Roebling Family Collection

stops.name: Brooklyn, the New York Bridge Company
stops.date_confidence: the incorporating act was approved 16 April 1867. The month of his appointment as chief engineer is contradicted between sources: NPS material implies May 1867, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge says September 1867. The contradiction is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: The New York State legislature approves the act incorporating the New York Bridge Company on the sixteenth of April, and the company makes him chief engineer. The sources disagree about the month of that appointment: some material implies May, the standard account of the bridge says September, and nobody has reconciled them. He is sixty-one. He has been arguing for this crossing since before the war, and he now has the commission, the capital, the son, and two years and three months.
suggested_refs: The act of 16 April 1867 incorporating the New York Bridge Company
sources: Rutgers Roebling Family Collection finding aid

stops.name: Fulton Ferry, the foot in the pilings
stops.date_confidence: 28 June 1869 attested; the toes were amputated afterward. Accounts differ slightly on the mechanism, between an arriving boat and the movement of the pilings themselves.
stops.campa: He is standing at the Fulton Ferry slip fixing the exact position of the Brooklyn tower, doing the thing he has done since he was nineteen, which is to measure ground before anybody builds on it. The timbers close on his right foot. Accounts differ on what moved, an arriving boat or the pilings themselves shifting in the rack, and no version has been settled against the others. Forty years of gorges and cable saddles and unfinished towers, and it happens at a landing stage. The toes are amputated on the twenty-eighth of June.
suggested_refs: The Fulton Ferry landing, Brooklyn, and the site of the Brooklyn tower

stops.name: Brooklyn Heights, the water cure
stops.date_confidence: July 1869 for the hydropathic treatment and the refusal of conventional care, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Roebling; the day is set only to order the stop between the injury and the death. His spiritualism, his reading of Swedenborg and Andrew Jackson Davis and his interest in mesmerism come from the dossier's own religion section and are reported rather than independently verified. Street-address coordinates are estimated along Hicks Street.
stops.campa: He is carried to his son's house in Brooklyn Heights and treats the crushed foot as he has treated every illness for thirty years, with water. Cold water poured over the wound continuously, restricted diet, and a refusal of most of what the surgeons propose. The water cure, the animal magnetism descended from Franz Anton Mesmer, the seance and the spiritualist library all belong to the same American middle of the century, and Roebling took the whole of it seriously enough to fill notebooks. The wound is a dockside crush injury and the tetanus is already in it.
suggested_refs: mesmer.journey.json, for the animal magnetism whose American descendants Roebling practised
Andrew Jackson Davis and the American water-cure literature of the 1840s and 1850s
sources: John A. Roebling dossier, religion and spiritualism section

stops.name: Hicks Street, tetanus
stops.date_confidence: 22 July 1869, of tetanus, at his son's house on Hicks Street in Brooklyn Heights, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Roebling; the twenty-four day interval from 28 June is correct. The house number 137, which circulates widely, is not in the cited source, and the source does not name Emily Warren Roebling as present.
stops.campa: Tetanus takes him twenty-four days after the ferry slip, in his son's house on Hicks Street, sixty-three years old. Washington inherits a chief engineership, a design on paper, and a bridge with not one stone laid. The house is the one Washington keeps with his wife Emily Warren Roebling, and within a few years she is the one carrying orders across the river from a sickroom window to a construction site, learning the mathematics as she goes. The number of the house is repeated everywhere and stands in no source reached here.
suggested_refs: The dossier for Emily Warren Roebling, working/journeys/dossiers/emily_roebling.dossier.md, a queued and unresearched subject

stops.name: Trenton, Riverview Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: July 1869 attested for the burial at Riverview Cemetery, Trenton; the exact day is not established and is set here after the 22 July death to order the segment. Coordinates 40.195, -74.754 per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverview_Cemetery_(Trenton,_New_Jersey); a figure 3.4 km north in the underlying afterlife notes is wrong.
stops.campa: The body goes back to Trenton, to the works and to the family plot at Riverview Cemetery above the Delaware. He is buried under the anglicized name he took in a Pennsylvania courtroom thirty-two years before. He had been in the country thirty-eight years, and had built five bridges of consequence and four canal aqueducts, founded a town, founded a factory, and left in a drawer somewhere between one and two thousand pages of philosophy. The exact day of the burial is not established. It falls in the last week of July 1869.
suggested_refs: The Roebling family plot, Riverview Cemetery, Trenton, New Jersey

stops.name: New York, Long and Short Span Railway Bridges
stops.date_confidence: 1869 publication year confirmed at Open Library across three editions; the D. Van Nostrand and New York imprint was not verified in this pass, and the Lehigh University Digital Bridges digitization returned HTTP 429 on refetch. Month set to place the stop after his death in July; whether it appeared before or after he died is not established.
stops.campa: His last book is published in New York in the year of his death, arguing the case for long spans against the multiplication of short ones. He wrote engineering the way he wrote everything, for print and for argument, and this half of the output did reach the public: the Niagara reports, the aqueduct specifications, the pamphlets on the East River. Whether the book reached the shops before the tetanus or after it is not established. Open Library holds three editions of it and gives no month for any of them.
suggested_refs: John A. Roebling, Long and Short Span Railway Bridges (1869), Open Library record
sources: Open Library, 'Long and Short Span Railway Bridges'

stops.name: Brooklyn, the bridge finished by his son
stops.date_confidence: construction began January 1870, six months after his death; the bridge opened 24 May 1883. The German Wikipedia claim that the Divi Blasii windows shaped the tower arches is tradition and is stated as such.
stops.campa: Construction begins in January 1870, six months after the burial, and the bridge opens on the twenty-fourth of May 1883, fourteen years after the death of the man who designed it. Washington runs the work from a window in Brooklyn Heights with caisson disease in his joints; Emily Warren Roebling carries the instructions, learns the mathematics, and faces down directors who want her husband replaced. The towers rise in granite and limestone with two pointed arches apiece, which is the shape a church at Mühlhausen is said to have put in his head.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_August_Röbling, on the claimed Divi Blasii window influence

stops.name: Trenton, the seated bronze in Cadwalader Park
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadwalader_Park confirms a seated bronze of Roebling erected in 1908 and does not name the sculptor. The 30 June date, the crowd of 15,000, the 6,500 marching employees, the governor, the Senate delegation and the Mühlhausen copper wreath all come from a todayinsci.com page that now returns HTTP 404 and are unsourced as of this pass. Coordinates corrected to 40.237, -74.79.
stops.campa: A seated bronze of him is put up in Cadwalader Park at Trenton, thirty-nine years after his death, in the city his factory built. The accounts of the unveiling describe a crowd past fifteen thousand, thousands of Roebling employees marching to the monument, the governor of New Jersey on the platform, and a copper wreath sent by Mühlhausen for its emigrant son. The page that carried those details has since gone off the web. What can still be confirmed is smaller: a statue, seated, 1908, in a public park.
suggested_refs: William Couper, sculptor, named in the 1908 accounts and not confirmed by any currently reachable source

stops.name: Trenton, the pages nobody has printed
stops.date_confidence: the 1958 division of the estate of John A. Roebling II between Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and Rutgers is described in the two finding aids; month and day defaulted. The pin is the Trenton desk where the manuscripts were written, not either repository, and no coordinate is asserted for Troy or New Brunswick. The page count is reported as roughly one thousand or roughly two thousand and has never been settled.
stops.campa: The unpublished philosophical manuscripts, never edited and never printed, are divided in 1958 between Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and Rutgers as the estate of his grandson is dispersed. The bridges are National Historic Landmarks by now and the wire rope has built an industry; the argument he was actually having, with Hegel, about spirit and matter, sits in two boxes in two states. Sources give the length as roughly a thousand pages, or roughly two thousand. The number has never been settled, and the reason it has never been settled is that nobody has read the whole of it through.
